title: God's Promise After the Flood
overview: After the flood, God renews his blessing, sets basic rules about blood and human life, and promises every creature never to flood the earth again, before a troubling episode in Noah's family ends in a curse.

parts.label: A fresh start (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: God repeats the creation blessing to have children and fill the earth. Animals will now fear people, and meat is allowed as food alongside plants, apparently for the first time.

parts.label: No meat with blood (v. 4)
parts.note: Meat must not be eaten with its lifeblood still in it, and the text links blood closely with life. It does not say why; interpreters have suggested it ruled out eating flesh from living animals, and later Israelite law tied blood to sacrifice.

parts.label: Every human life counts (vv. 5-7)
parts.note: God says he will call to account any animal or person that takes a human life. Verse 6 adds that whoever kills a person will have their own blood shed by people, because humans are made in God's image.

parts.label: A promise and a rainbow (vv. 8-17)
parts.note: God makes a covenant, a solemn binding promise, with Noah's family and every living creature, with no conditions attached: never again will a flood destroy all life. The rainbow is its sign, and because the Hebrew word also means a warrior's bow, some scholars read it as a weapon hung up in peace.

parts.label: Noah drunk in his tent (vv. 18-23)
parts.note: Noah gets drunk on wine from his vineyard and lies naked in his tent. Ham sees him and tells his brothers, who walk in backward to cover him; most read Ham's wrong as mocking disrespect, though similar wording elsewhere in the Bible can hint at a sexual wrong, and scholars are unsure.

parts.label: Curse and blessings (vv. 24-29)
parts.note: Noah curses Ham's son Canaan to serve his brothers and blesses Shem and Japheth; the text never says why Canaan rather than Ham is cursed, and many scholars read it as reflecting Israel's later rule over the Canaanites. Centuries later this was used to defend enslaving Africans, but the curse names only Canaan and says nothing about Africa or skin color.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether verse 6 sets a lasting rule that supports the death penalty or mainly declares the worth of every human life without requiring execution today.
think: When someone you respect fails badly, what do you think you owe them, and what do you owe the truth?
